claim: The dorsal raphe nucleus is the predominant source of central serotonin.
source: The dorsal raphe nucleus is the predominant source of central serotonin, where neuronal activity regulates complex emotional behaviors.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific citation in this sentence.

claim: Neuronal activity in the dorsal raphe nucleus regulates complex emotional behaviors.
source: The dorsal raphe nucleus is the predominant source of central serotonin, where neuronal activity regulates complex emotional behaviors.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Action potential firing of serotonin dorsal raphe neurons is driven via α1-adrenergic receptors (α1-AR) activation.
source: Action potential firing of serotonin dorsal raphe neurons is driven via α1-adrenergic receptors (α1-AR) activation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: The ion channels responsible for α1-AR-mediated depolarization in dorsal raphe neurons were unknown prior to this study.
source: Despite this crucial role, the ion channels responsible for α1-AR-mediated depolarization are unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the abstract.

claim: α1-AR-mediated excitatory synaptic transmission in mouse dorsal raphe neurons is mediated by GluD1R-channels.
source: Here, we show in mouse brain slices that α1-AR-mediated excitatory synaptic transmission is mediated by the ionotropic glutamate receptor homolog cation channel, delta glutamate receptor 1 (GluD1).
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the results section.

claim: GluD1R-channels are constitutively active under basal conditions carrying tonic inward current.
source: GluD1R-channels are constitutively active under basal conditions carrying tonic inward current and synaptic activation of α1-ARs augments tonic GluD1R-channel current.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing NASPM-sensitive tonic current in Figure 3.

claim: Synaptic activation of α1-ARs augments tonic GluD1R-channel current.
source: GluD1R-channels are constitutively active under basal conditions carrying tonic inward current and synaptic activation of α1-ARs augments tonic GluD1R-channel current.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased current during α1-AR-EPSC in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Loss of dorsal raphe GluD1R-channels produces an anxiogenic phenotype.
source: Further, loss of dorsal raphe GluD1R-channels produces an anxiogenic phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data in Figure 6 showing reduced time in open arms of elevated plus maze.

claim: GluD1R-channels are responsible for α1-AR-dependent induction of persistent pacemaker-type firing of dorsal raphe neurons.
source: Thus, GluD1R-channels are responsible for α1-AR-dependent induction of persistent pacemaker-type firing of dorsal raphe neurons and regulate dorsal raphe-related behavior.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that α1-AR activation produces prolonged firing (Figure 1) and that GluD1R deletion eliminates the α1-AR-EPSC (Figure 5).

claim: GluD1R-channels regulate dorsal raphe-related behavior.
source: Thus, GluD1R-channels are responsible for α1-AR-dependent induction of persistent pacemaker-type firing of dorsal raphe neurons and regulate dorsal raphe-related behavior.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data in Figure 6.

claim: Ion channel function of GluD1R as a regulator of neuronal excitability is proposed to be widespread in the nervous system.
source: Given the widespread distribution of these channels, ion channel function of GluD1R as a regulator of neuronal excitability is proposed to be widespread in the nervous system.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the widespread distribution of GluD1R.

claim: 1 in 5 adults worldwide are affected by a mental health disorder.
source: Recent reports estimate that 1 in 5 adults worldwide are affected by a mental health disorder, with anxiety and depression being the most common affecting more than 260 million people (GBD 2017 Disease and Injury Incidence and Prevalence Collaborators, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to GBD 2017 Disease and Injury Incidence and Prevalence Collaborators, 2018.

claim: Anxiety and depression are the most common mental health disorders affecting more than 260 million people.
source: Recent reports estimate that 1 in 5 adults worldwide are affected by a mental health disorder, with anxiety and depression being the most common affecting more than 260 million people (GBD 2017 Disease and Injury Incidence and Prevalence Collaborators, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to GBD 2017 Disease and Injury Incidence and Prevalence Collaborators, 2018.

claim: Most current pharmacotherapies to treat anxiety and depression target serotonin receptors or serotonin clearance.
source: Most current pharmacotherapies to treat these disorders target serotonin receptors or serotonin clearance.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The dorsal raphe nucleus is the largest serotonergic nucleus in the brain.
source: The dorsal raphe nucleus is the largest serotonergic nucleus in the brain and the predominant source of central serotonin (5-HT).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: In vivo, tonic noradrenergic input to the dorsal raphe that activates α1-adrenergic receptors is required for 5-HT neurons to fire action potentials.
source: In vivo, tonic noradrenergic input to the dorsal raphe that activates Gαq/11 protein-coupled α1-adrenergic receptors (α1-ARs) is required for 5-HT neurons to fire action potentials (Baraban and Aghajanian, 1980; Baraban et al., 1978) and release 5-HT (Clement et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Baraban and Aghajanian, 1980; Baraban et al., 1978.

claim: Tonic noradrenergic input to the dorsal raphe that activates α1-adrenergic receptors is required for 5-HT release.
source: In vivo, tonic noradrenergic input to the dorsal raphe that activates Gαq/11 protein-coupled α1-adrenergic receptors (α1-ARs) is required for 5-HT neurons to fire action potentials (Baraban and Aghajanian, 1980; Baraban et al., 1978) and release 5-HT (Clement et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Clement et al., 1992.

claim: In dorsal raphe brain slices, synaptic activation of α1-ARs produces a slow membrane depolarization lasting tens of seconds.
source: In dorsal raphe brain slices, synaptic activation of α1-ARs produces a slow membrane depolarization lasting tens of seconds (Yoshimura et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yoshimura et al., 1985.

claim: Activation of Gαq/11 protein-coupled receptors produces slow, noisy inward currents throughout the central and peripheral nervous system.
source: Throughout the central and peripheral nervous system, activation of Gαq/11 protein-coupled receptors (GqPCRs), namely metabotropic glutamate mGluRs, muscarinic acetylcholine M1 (mAChRs), or α1-ARs produces slow, noisy inward currents.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Multiple mechanisms have been reported to underlie GqPCR-mediated inward current including inhibition of K+ current.
source: Multiple mechanisms have been reported to underlie the inward current including: inhibition of K+ current (including leak, Ca2+-activated, and Kv7/M-current) (Benson et al., 1988; Halliwell and Adams, 1982; Madison et al., 1987; Shen and North, 1992), modulation of TTX-sensitive persistent Na+ current (Yamada-Hanff and Bean, 2013), and activation of transient potential receptor canonical (TRPC) (Hartmann et al., 2008; Kim et al., 2003), Na+-leak (NALCN) (Lu et al., 2009), or delta glutamate receptor-channels (Ady et al., 2014; Benamer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Multiple mechanisms have been reported to underlie GqPCR-mediated inward current including modulation of TTX-sensitive persistent Na+ current.
source: Multiple mechanisms have been reported to underlie the inward current including: inhibition of K+ current (including leak, Ca2+-activated, and Kv7/M-current) (Benson et al., 1988; Halliwell and Adams, 1982; Madison et al., 1987; Shen and North, 1992), modulation of TTX-sensitive persistent Na+ current (Yamada-Hanff and Bean, 2013), and activation of transient potential receptor canonical (TRPC) (Hartmann et al., 2008; Kim et al., 2003), Na+-leak (NALCN) (Lu et al., 2009), or delta glutamate receptor-channels (Ady et al., 2014; Benamer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yamada-Hanff and Bean, 2013.

claim: Multiple mechanisms have been reported to underlie GqPCR-mediated inward current including activation of TRPC channels.
source: Multiple mechanisms have been reported to underlie the inward current including: inhibition of K+ current (including leak, Ca2+-activated, and Kv7/M-current) (Benson et al., 1988; Halliwell and Adams, 1982; Madison et al., 1987; Shen and North, 1992), modulation of TTX-sensitive persistent Na+ current (Yamada-Hanff and Bean, 2013), and activation of transient potential receptor canonical (TRPC) (Hartmann et al., 2008; Kim et al., 2003), Na+-leak (NALCN) (Lu et al., 2009), or delta glutamate receptor-channels (Ady et al., 2014; Benamer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hartmann et al., 2008; Kim et al., 2003.

claim: Multiple mechanisms have been reported to underlie GqPCR-mediated inward current including activation of NALCN channels.
source: Multiple mechanisms have been reported to underlie the inward current including: inhibition of K+ current (including leak, Ca2+-activated, and Kv7/M-current) (Benson et al., 1988; Halliwell and Adams, 1982; Madison et al., 1987; Shen and North, 1992), modulation of TTX-sensitive persistent Na+ current (Yamada-Hanff and Bean, 2013), and activation of transient potential receptor canonical (TRPC) (Hartmann et al., 2008; Kim et al., 2003), Na+-leak (NALCN) (Lu et al., 2009), or delta glutamate receptor-channels (Ady et al., 2014; Benamer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lu et al., 2009.

claim: Multiple mechanisms have been reported to underlie GqPCR-mediated inward current including activation of delta glutamate receptor-channels.
source: Multiple mechanisms have been reported to underlie the inward current including: inhibition of K+ current (including leak, Ca2+-activated, and Kv7/M-current) (Benson et al., 1988; Halliwell and Adams, 1982; Madison et al., 1987; Shen and North, 1992), modulation of TTX-sensitive persistent Na+ current (Yamada-Hanff and Bean, 2013), and activation of transient potential receptor canonical (TRPC) (Hartmann et al., 2008; Kim et al., 2003), Na+-leak (NALCN) (Lu et al., 2009), or delta glutamate receptor-channels (Ady et al., 2014; Benamer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ady et al., 2014; Benamer et al., 2018.

claim: Delta glutamate receptors GluD1R and GluD2R are not gated by glutamate.
source: The delta glutamate receptors, GluD1R and GluD2R, are mysterious members of the ionotropic glutamate receptor family in that they are not gated by glutamate (Araki et al., 1993; Lomeli et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Araki et al., 1993; Lomeli et al., 1993.

claim: One theory is that delta glutamate receptors are strictly scaffolding proteins or synaptic organizers, rather than ion conducting channels.
source: One theory is that they are strictly scaffolding proteins or synaptic organizers, rather than ion conducting channels.
evidence: This is stated as a theory in the field.

claim: Wild-type delta glutamate receptor channels have been reported to conduct in response to activation of mGluRs.
source: But wild-type channels have been reported to conduct in response to activation of mGluRs (Ady et al., 2014; Benamer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ady et al., 2014; Benamer et al., 2018.

claim: GluD1R (Grid1) mRNA is expressed widely throughout the brain.
source: GluD1R (Grid1) mRNA is expressed widely throughout the brain, with notably high levels in the dorsal raphe (Hepp et al., 2015; Konno et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hepp et al., 2015; Konno et al., 2014.

claim: GluD1R (Grid1) mRNA is expressed at notably high levels in the dorsal raphe.
source: GluD1R (Grid1) mRNA is expressed widely throughout the brain, with notably high levels in the dorsal raphe (Hepp et al., 2015; Konno et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hepp et al., 2015; Konno et al., 2014.

claim: A train of 5 electrical stimuli at 60 Hz produced firing in previously quiescent dorsal raphe neurons.
source: With cell-attached recordings, a train of 5 electrical stimuli (60 Hz), delivered to the brain slice via a monopolar stimulating electrode, produced firing in previously quiescent neurons, which was blocked by application of the α1-AR antagonist, prazosin (100 nM, Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Electrical stimulation-induced firing in dorsal raphe neurons was blocked by the α1-AR antagonist prazosin.
source: With cell-attached recordings, a train of 5 electrical stimuli (60 Hz), delivered to the brain slice via a monopolar stimulating electrode, produced firing in previously quiescent neurons, which was blocked by application of the α1-AR antagonist, prazosin (100 nM, Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Electrical stimulation produced 20±5 action potentials in dorsal raphe neurons.
source: The excitation produced 20±5 action potentials that lasted 9.0±3.0 s, with a latency of 650.6±0.1 ms from onset of stimulation to the first action potential (Figure 1B-E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-E.

claim: Electrical stimulation-induced action potential firing in dorsal raphe neurons lasted 9.0±3.0 s.
source: The excitation produced 20±5 action potentials that lasted 9.0±3.0 s, with a latency of 650.6±0.1 ms from onset of stimulation to the first action potential (Figure 1B-E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-E.

claim: The latency from onset of stimulation to the first action potential was 650.6±0.1 ms.
source: The excitation produced 20±5 action potentials that lasted 9.0±3.0 s, with a latency of 650.6±0.1 ms from onset of stimulation to the first action potential (Figure 1B-E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-E.

claim: Electrical stimulation produced a slow and long-lasting EPSC with duration of 27.4±2.3 s in voltage-clamp mode.
source: In voltage-clamp mode (Vhold -65 mV), the same stimulation produced a slow and long-lasting (27.4±2.3 s, n=10) excitatory postsynaptic current (EPSC, Figure 1F) that was eliminated by the application of prazosin (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The α1-AR-EPSC was eliminated by the application of prazosin.
source: In voltage-clamp mode (Vhold -65 mV), the same stimulation produced a slow and long-lasting (27.4±2.3 s, n=10) excitatory postsynaptic current (EPSC, Figure 1F) that was eliminated by the application of prazosin (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Prazosin had no effect on basal whole-cell current.
source: Prazosin had no effect on basal whole-cell current (-3.8±3.4 pA, p=0.232, n=10, data not shown) indicating a lack of persistent inward current due to noradrenaline tone.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: The duration of the α1-AR-EPSC was orders of magnitude longer than fast AMPAR channel-mediated EPSCs (~103.5×).
source: On average, the duration of the α1-AR-EPSC was orders of magnitude longer than fast AMPAR channel-mediated EPSCs (~103.5×) and ~18× longer than 'slow' 5-HT1A receptor-G protein-coupled inwardly rectifying potassium channel (GIRK)-dependent IPSCs (Gantz et al., 2015a; Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H and comparison with cited data.

claim: The duration of the α1-AR-EPSC was ~18× longer than 5-HT1A receptor-GIRK-dependent IPSCs.
source: On average, the duration of the α1-AR-EPSC was orders of magnitude longer than fast AMPAR channel-mediated EPSCs (~103.5×) and ~18× longer than 'slow' 5-HT1A receptor-G protein-coupled inwardly rectifying potassium channel (GIRK)-dependent IPSCs (Gantz et al., 2015a; Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H and comparison with cited data.

claim: Disruption of G protein signaling with intracellular dialysis of GDPβS-Li3 eliminated the α1-AR-EPSC within 5-20 mins post-break-in.
source: Disruption of G protein signaling with intracellular dialysis of GDPβS-Li3 eliminated the α1-AR-EPSC within 5-20 mins post-break-in (p=0.004, n=9), whereas dialysis with LiCl alone had no effect on the amplitude of the α1-AR-EPSC (p=0.625, n=4, Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Dialysis with LiCl alone had no effect on the amplitude of the α1-AR-EPSC.
source: Disruption of G protein signaling with intracellular dialysis of GDPβS-Li3 eliminated the α1-AR-EPSC within 5-20 mins post-break-in (p=0.004, n=9), whereas dialysis with LiCl alone had no effect on the amplitude of the α1-AR-EPSC (p=0.625, n=4, Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The α1-AR-EPSC has a cell-autonomous requirement of G protein signaling.
source: These findings demonstrate a cell-autonomous requirement of G protein signaling in the generation of the α1-AR-EPSC.
evidence: This is inferred from the GDPβS-Li3 experiment shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Application of tetrodotoxin reversibly abolished the α1-AR-EPSC.
source: Application of tetrodotoxin (1 μM) reversibly abolished the α1-AR-EPSC, demonstrating a dependence on presynaptic action potentials (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: The α1-AR-EPSC is dependent on presynaptic action potentials.
source: Application of tetrodotoxin (1 μM) reversibly abolished the α1-AR-EPSC, demonstrating a dependence on presynaptic action potentials (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is inferred from the tetrodotoxin experiment shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Disruption of the vesicular monoamine transporter with reserpine eliminated the α1-AR-EPSC.
source: Disruption of the vesicular monoamine transporter with reserpine (1 μM) or removal of external Ca2+ also eliminated the α1-AR-EPSC, indicating noradrenaline release is vesicular (Figure 1K and L).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: Removal of external Ca2+ eliminated the α1-AR-EPSC.
source: Disruption of the vesicular monoamine transporter with reserpine (1 μM) or removal of external Ca2+ also eliminated the α1-AR-EPSC, indicating noradrenaline release is vesicular (Figure 1K and L).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1L.

claim: Noradrenaline release underlying the α1-AR-EPSC is vesicular.
source: Disruption of the vesicular monoamine transporter with reserpine (1 μM) or removal of external Ca2+ also eliminated the α1-AR-EPSC, indicating noradrenaline release is vesicular (Figure 1K and L).
evidence: This is inferred from the reserpine and Ca2+ removal experiments shown in Figure 1K and L.

claim: Membrane resistance significantly decreased during the α1-AR-EPSC.
source: Under our recording conditions, resistance of the membrane (Rm) significantly decreased during the α1-AR-EPSC, indicative of opening of ion channels (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The decrease in membrane resistance during the α1-AR-EPSC is indicative of opening of ion channels.
source: Under our recording conditions, resistance of the membrane (Rm) significantly decreased during the α1-AR-EPSC, indicative of opening of ion channels (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is inferred from the decrease in membrane resistance shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Membrane noise variance increased significantly during the α1-AR-EPSC compared to basal conditions.
source: Membrane noise variance (σ2) increased significantly during the EPSC compared to membrane noise under basal conditions (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: The α1-AR-EPSC σ2 – amplitude relationship was well fit by linear regression, yielding an estimate of a -1.16 pA unitary current.
source: The α1-AR-EPSC σ2 – amplitude relationship was well fit by linear regression, suggestive of a consistent conductance state, yielding an estimate of a -1.16 pA unitary current (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The α1-AR-EPSC reversed polarity at -28.6±2.4 mV.
source: Voltage ramps from -120 to -10 mV (1 mV/10 ms) before and during the α1-AR-EPSC (Figure 2E) showed that the current reversed polarity at -28.6±2.4 mV (Figure 2E-G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E-G.

claim: Exogenous application of noradrenaline produced an inward current with a reversal potential of -25.1±2.9 mV.
source: Exogenous application of noradrenaline (30 μM, in the presence of α2-AR antagonist, idazoxan, 1 μM) produced an inward current (INA) with a similar reversal potential (-25.1±2.9 mV, Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Replacing extracellular Na+ with NMDG completely abolished inward INA.
source: Replacing extracellular Na+ (126 mM) with N-methyl D-glucamine (NMDG) completely abolished inward INA, suggesting Na+ as the prominent charge carrier (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Na+ is the prominent charge carrier for the noradrenaline-induced inward current.
source: Replacing extracellular Na+ (126 mM) with N-methyl D-glucamine (NMDG) completely abolished inward INA, suggesting Na+ as the prominent charge carrier (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is inferred from the NMDG substitution experiment shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Increasing extracellular K+ from 2.5 to 6.5 or 10.5 mM had no effect on the amplitude of the α1-AR-EPSC at Vhold -65 mV.
source: Increasing extracellular K+ from 2.5 to 6.5 or 10.5 mM, expected to shift Ek from -107 to -81 and -69 mV, respectively, had no effect on the amplitude of the α1-AR-EPSC at Vhold -65 mV (Figure 2I) nor -120 mV (p=0.692, n=11, data not shown), but produced a significant depolarizing shift in Erev of the α1-AR-EPSC (Figure 2J), suggesting the channel is also permeable to K+, and may be 2-3× as permeable to K+ as Na+.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Increasing extracellular K+ produced a significant depolarizing shift in Erev of the α1-AR-EPSC.
source: Increasing extracellular K+ from 2.5 to 6.5 or 10.5 mM, expected to shift Ek from -107 to -81 and -69 mV, respectively, had no effect on the amplitude of the α1-AR-EPSC at Vhold -65 mV (Figure 2I) nor -120 mV (p=0.692, n=11, data not shown), but produced a significant depolarizing shift in Erev of the α1-AR-EPSC (Figure 2J), suggesting the channel is also permeable to K+, and may be 2-3× as permeable to K+ as Na+.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: The channel underlying the α1-AR-EPSC is permeable to K+.
source: Increasing extracellular K+ from 2.5 to 6.5 or 10.5 mM, expected to shift Ek from -107 to -81 and -69 mV, respectively, had no effect on the amplitude of the α1-AR-EPSC at Vhold -65 mV (Figure 2I) nor -120 mV (p=0.692, n=11, data not shown), but produced a significant depolarizing shift in Erev of the α1-AR-EPSC (Figure 2J), suggesting the channel is also permeable to K+, and may be 2-3× as permeable to K+ as Na+.
evidence: This is inferred from the shift in Erev with changing K+ shown in Figure 2J.

claim: The channel underlying the α1-AR-EPSC may be 2-3× as permeable to K+ as Na+.
source: Increasing extracellular K+ from 2.5 to 6.5 or 10.5 mM, expected to shift Ek from -107 to -81 and -69 mV, respectively, had no effect on the amplitude of the α1-AR-EPSC at Vhold -65 mV (Figure 2I) nor -120 mV (p=0.692, n=11, data not shown), but produced a significant depolarizing shift in Erev of the α1-AR-EPSC (Figure 2J), suggesting the channel is also permeable to K+, and may be 2-3× as permeable to K+ as Na+.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the shift in Erev with changing K+ shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Removal of external MgCl2 had no significant effect on Erev of INA.
source: Removal of external MgCl2 had no significant effect on Erev (-28.5±5.7 mV), nor on the amplitude of INA (Figure 2K and L).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: Removal of external MgCl2 had no significant effect on the amplitude of INA.
source: Removal of external MgCl2 had no significant effect on Erev (-28.5±5.7 mV), nor on the amplitude of INA (Figure 2K and L).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2L.

claim: Removal of external CaCl2 had no effect on Erev of INA.
source: Removal of external CaCl2 also had no effect on Erev (-30.3±3.5 mV) but significantly augmented inward INA, (Figure 2K and L).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: Removal of external CaCl2 significantly augmented inward INA.
source: Removal of external CaCl2 also had no effect on Erev (-30.3±3.5 mV) but significantly augmented inward INA, (Figure 2K and L).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2L.

claim: α1-AR-dependent current is carried through a mixed cation channel, with inward current carried predominantly by Na+ entry.
source: Taken together, the data suggest that α1-AR-dependent current, whether produced by vesicular release of noradrenaline or exogenous noradrenaline application is carried through a mixed cation channel, with inward current carried predominantly by Na+ entry.
evidence: This is inferred from the ion substitution experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Conditioning depolarizing pre-pulses incrementally reduced GNA measured at Vhold -120 mV.
source: Conditioning depolarizing pre-pulses incrementally reduced GNA and the increase in membrane noise induced by noradrenaline measured at Vhold -120 mV (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D), demonstrating voltage-dependence of inward INA, such that depolarization reduced conductance.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Conditioning depolarizing pre-pulses incrementally reduced the increase in membrane noise induced by noradrenaline measured at Vhold -120 mV.
source: Conditioning depolarizing pre-pulses incrementally reduced GNA and the increase in membrane noise induced by noradrenaline measured at Vhold -120 mV (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D), demonstrating voltage-dependence of inward INA, such that depolarization reduced conductance.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Inward INA demonstrates voltage-dependence, such that depolarization reduced conductance.
source: Conditioning depolarizing pre-pulses incrementally reduced GNA and the increase in membrane noise induced by noradrenaline measured at Vhold -120 mV (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D), demonstrating voltage-dependence of inward INA, such that depolarization reduced conductance.
evidence: This is inferred from the pre-pulse experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Application of NASPM blocked the α1-AR-EPSC by 96.0 ± 12.5%.
source: Application of NASPM (100 μM, 6 min) blocked the α1-AR-EPSC (96.0 ± 12.5% reduction), which recovered to baseline after a wash of >30 mins (Figures 3A, B, E and I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3A, B, E and I.

claim: The α1-AR-EPSC recovered to baseline after a wash of >30 mins following NASPM application.
source: Application of NASPM (100 μM, 6 min) blocked the α1-AR-EPSC (96.0 ± 12.5% reduction), which recovered to baseline after a wash of >30 mins (Figures 3A, B, E and I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3A, B, E and I.

claim: NASPM produced an apparent outward current (INSP) of 20.5 ± 3.7 pA with an Erev of −31.4 ± 4.8 mV.
source: NASPM also produced an apparent outward current (INSP) of 20.5 ± 3.7 pA with an Erev of −31.4 ± 4.8 mV (Figures 3A, C, E and G) and a reduction in membrane noise (Figure 3A and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3A, C, E and G.

claim: NASPM produced a reduction in membrane noise.
source: NASPM also produced an apparent outward current (INSP) of 20.5 ± 3.7 pA with an Erev of −31.4 ± 4.8 mV (Figures 3A, C, E and G) and a reduction in membrane noise (Figure 3A and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and D.

claim: INSP reversed with a similar time course of recovery of the α1-AR-EPSC after washout.
source: After washout, INSP reversed with a similar time course of recovery of the α1-AR-EPSC (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: INSP was associated with an increase in Rm indicating a closure of channels.
source: INSP was associated with an increase in Rm (Figure 3F) indicating a closure of channels.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and inferred from the increase in Rm.

claim: Replacing extracellular Na+ with NMDG eliminated INSP.
source: Replacing extracellular Na+ (126 mM) with NMDG eliminated INSP (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: INSP was due to block of tonic Na+-dependent inward current.
source: Thus, INSP was due to block of tonic Na+-dependent inward current.
evidence: This is inferred from the NMDG substitution experiment shown in Figure 3G.

claim: INSP was not dependent on prior electrical stimulation of the brain slice.
source: INSP was not dependent on prior electrical stimulation of the brain slice, as the magnitude of INSP was similar between stimulated and unstimulated brain slices (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The α1-AR-EPSC was blocked by NASPM without requiring electrical stimulation during NASPM application.
source: After obtaining a steady α1-AR-EPSC baseline, NASPM was applied for 6 min without stimulating the brain slice. The α1-AR-EPSC was blocked when stimulation was reapplied (Figure 3I), indicating that the channels underlying the α1-AR-EPSC were already blocked.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The channels underlying the α1-AR-EPSC are at least transiently open at rest.
source: Thus, the α1-AR-EPSC is mediated by channels that are at least transiently open at rest and may be the same channels underlie the apparent outward current induced by NASPM.
evidence: This is inferred from the NASPM block experiment shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The channels underlying the α1-AR-EPSC may be the same channels that underlie the apparent outward current induced by NASPM.
source: Thus, the α1-AR-EPSC is mediated by channels that are at least transiently open at rest and may be the same channels underlie the apparent outward current induced by NASPM.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the similar properties of the α1-AR-EPSC and INSP.

claim: Application of D-serine reduced the amplitude of the α1-AR-EPSC by 49.7 ± 9.6%.
source: Application of D-serine (10 mM, 13.5 min) reduced the amplitude of the α1-AR-EPSC by 49.7 ± 9.6% (Figure 4A and E), without affecting unitary channel current (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and E.

claim: D-serine did not affect unitary channel current of the α1-AR-EPSC.
source: Application of D-serine (10 mM, 13.5 min) reduced the amplitude of the α1-AR-EPSC by 49.7 ± 9.6% (Figure 4A and E), without affecting unitary channel current (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Application of glycine reduced the amplitude of the α1-AR-EPSC by 70.9 ± 11.0%.
source: Application of glycine (10 mM, 4.5 mins, in the presence of the glycine receptor antagonist, strychnine (10 μM), also reduced the amplitude of the α1-AR-EPSC by 70.9 ± 11.0% (Figure 4C and E), without affecting unitary channel current (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and E.

claim: Glycine did not affect unitary channel current of the α1-AR-EPSC.
source: Application of glycine (10 mM, 4.5 mins, in the presence of the glycine receptor antagonist, strychnine (10 μM), also reduced the amplitude of the α1-AR-EPSC by 70.9 ± 11.0% (Figure 4C and E), without affecting unitary channel current (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Application of kynurenic acid reduced the α1-AR-EPSC amplitude by 65.6 ± 8.3%.
source: Lastly, we found that application of the glutamate receptor antagonist kynurenic acid (1 mM, 10.5 min) reduced the α1-AR-EPSC amplitude by 65.6 ± 8.3% (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Restriction enzyme site-digested PCR confirmed in vivo mutation of Grid1 at the expected site.
source: Brain slices were prepared after >4 weeks and the dorsal raphe was microdissected and frozen on dry ice to assess the mutation of Grid1. Restriction enzyme site-digested PCR confirmed in vivo mutation of Grid1 at the expected site (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: In eGFP+ neurons from control mice, electrical stimulation produced a decrease in Rm and an α1-AR-EPSC.
source: In eGFP+ neurons from control mice, electrical stimulation produced a decrease in Rm and an α1-AR-EPSC, and bath application of noradrenaline caused inward INA (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: In eGFP+ neurons from control mice, bath application of noradrenaline caused inward INA.
source: In eGFP+ neurons from control mice, electrical stimulation produced a decrease in Rm and an α1-AR-EPSC, and bath application of noradrenaline caused inward INA (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: In eGFP+ neurons from Grid1 mice, electrical stimulation did not change Rm.
source: However, in eGFP+ neurons from Grid1 mice, electrical stimulation did not change Rm (Figure 5A) and no α1-AR-EPSC was detected above baseline noise (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In eGFP+ neurons from Grid1 mice, no α1-AR-EPSC was detected above baseline noise.
source: However, in eGFP+ neurons from Grid1 mice, electrical stimulation did not change Rm (Figure 5A) and no α1-AR-EPSC was detected above baseline noise (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: Inward INA was substantially smaller in eGFP+ neurons from Grid1 mice compared to eGFP+ neurons from control mice.
source: In addition, inward INA was substantially smaller in eGFP+ neurons from Grid1 mice, as compared to eGFP+ neurons from control mice (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: In the same slices from Grid1 mice, eGFP- neurons still had an α1-AR-EPSC and inward INA.
source: In the same slices from Grid1 mice, eGFP- neurons still had an α1-AR-EPSC and inward INA (Figure 5B and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and D.

claim: Bath application of NASPM produced an apparent outward current in eGFP+ neurons from control mice, but not from Grid1 mice.
source: Lastly, bath application of NASPM produced an apparent outward current in eGFP+ neurons from control mice, but not from Grid1 mice (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Conduction through GluD1R-channels is necessary for the α1-AR-EPSC.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that conduction through GluD1R-channels is necessary for the α1-AR-EPSC and the NASPM-sensitive tonic inward current.
evidence: This is inferred from the CRISPR/Cas9 experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Conduction through GluD1R-channels is necessary for the NASPM-sensitive tonic inward current.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that conduction through GluD1R-channels is necessary for the α1-AR-EPSC and the NASPM-sensitive tonic inward current.
evidence: This is inferred from the CRISPR/Cas9 experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: There was no difference in total distance traveled between control and Grid1 mice in a dark arena.
source: Basal locomotion was assayed in a dark arena. There was no difference between the two groups in the total distance traveled (Figure 6B) nor in the velocity of movements between control and Grid1 mice (p=0.772, n = 18 and 16, data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: There was no difference in velocity of movements between control and Grid1 mice in a dark arena.
source: Basal locomotion was assayed in a dark arena. There was no difference between the two groups in the total distance traveled (Figure 6B) nor in the velocity of movements between control and Grid1 mice (p=0.772, n = 18 and 16, data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data.

claim: Grid1 mice spent less time in the open arms of the elevated plus maze compared to control mice.
source: Grid1 mice spent less time in the open arms when compared to control mice (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6C–E.

claim: Control and Grid1 mice made a similar total number of entries to either open or enclosed arms of the elevated plus maze.
source: Control and Grid1 mice made a similar total number of entries to either open or enclosed arms (control: 39.4 ± 2.0; Grid1: 36.0 ± 2.3, p=0.697), but Grid1 mice made proportionally fewer entries to the open arms (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Grid1 mice made proportionally fewer entries to the open arms of the elevated plus maze.
source: Control and Grid1 mice made a similar total number of entries to either open or enclosed arms (control: 39.4 ± 2.0; Grid1: 36.0 ± 2.3, p=0.697), but Grid1 mice made proportionally fewer entries to the open arms (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Time spent grooming was similar between control and Grid1 mice in the elevated plus maze.
source: Time spent grooming or in stretched-attend postures were similar between control and Grid1 mice (Figure 6F and G).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Time spent in stretched-attend postures was similar between control and Grid1 mice in the elevated plus maze.
source: Time spent grooming or in stretched-attend postures were similar between control and Grid1 mice (Figure 6F and G).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Grid1 mice spent less time lowering their head over the edge of the open arms (head-dipping) than control mice.
source: Grid1 mice spent less time lowering their head over the edge of the open arms than control mice (head-dipping, Figure 6H), suggestive of decreased exploratory behavior.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Decreased head-dipping in Grid1 mice is suggestive of decreased exploratory behavior.
source: Grid1 mice spent less time lowering their head over the edge of the open arms than control mice (head-dipping, Figure 6H), suggestive of decreased exploratory behavior.
evidence: This is inferred from the decreased head-dipping behavior shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Grid1 mice spent a similar amount of time rearing in the enclosed arms compared to control mice.
source: However, Grid1 mice spent a similar amount of time rearing in the enclosed arms compared to control mice (Figure 6I) suggesting innate exploratory drive in the enclosed arms was intact.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Innate exploratory drive in the enclosed arms was intact in Grid1 mice.
source: However, Grid1 mice spent a similar amount of time rearing in the enclosed arms compared to control mice (Figure 6I) suggesting innate exploratory drive in the enclosed arms was intact.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar rearing behavior shown in Figure 6I.

claim: The behavioral results are indicative of heightened anxiety after functional deletion of GluD1R-channels in the dorsal raphe.
source: Taken together, these results are indicative of heightened anxiety after functional deletion of GluD1R-channels in the dorsal raphe.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral data shown in Figure 6.

claim: In vivo, 5-HT neurons in the dorsal raphe require noradrenaline release and subsequent activation of α1-ARs to maintain persistent action potential firing.
source: In vivo, 5-HT neurons in the dorsal raphe require noradrenaline release and subsequent activation of α1-ARs to maintain persistent action potential firing (Baraban and Aghajanian, 1980).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Baraban and Aghajanian, 1980.

claim: Activation of α1-ARs in the dorsal raphe was thought to depolarize neurons through net reduction of K+ conductance.
source: The activation of α1-ARs in the dorsal raphe by exogenous agonist was thought to depolarize neurons through net reduction of K+ conductance, transiently activating calcium-activated K+ current while persistently decreasing another K+ current, and by activation of an unidentified non-K+ conductance (Pan et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pan et al., 1994.

claim: Brown et al. (2002) reported that activation of α1-ARs induces Na+-dependent inward current with an Erev of −23 mV in the dorsal raphe.
source: In a more recent study in the dorsal raphe, Brown et al. (2002) reported that activation of α1-ARs, induces Na+-dependent inward current with an Erev of −23 mV, similar to our findings.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brown et al. (2002).

claim: Modulation of GluD1R-channels is a key constituent in driving persistent action potential firing of 5-HT neurons.
source: Our study identifies GluD1 receptor-channels as the ion channel that carries this mixed cation current, indicating that modulation of GluD1R-channels is a key constituent in driving persistent action potential firing of the 5-HT neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing GluD1R-channels mediate the α1-AR-EPSC.

claim: Inward GluD1R-channel current may bring the membrane potential to threshold.
source: In principle, inward GluD1R-channel current may bring the membrane potential to threshold, but recruitment of other voltage-gated ion channels is expected to underlie the persistent pacemaker-like activity.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the properties of GluD1R-channels.

claim: Recruitment of other voltage-gated ion channels is expected to underlie the persistent pacemaker-like activity of dorsal raphe neurons.
source: In principle, inward GluD1R-channel current may bring the membrane potential to threshold, but recruitment of other voltage-gated ion channels is expected to underlie the persistent pacemaker-like activity.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the properties of GluD1R-channels.

claim: Brown et al. (2002) demonstrated that activation of Gq protein-coupled histamine H1 and orexin OX2 receptors produced an inward current that was occluded by the α1-AR-dependent current.
source: Intriguingly, Brown et al. (2002) demonstrated that activation of Gq protein-coupled histamine H1 and orexin OX2 receptors also produced an inward current that was occluded by the α1-AR-dependent current.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brown et al. (2002).

claim: Whether histamine H1 and orexin OX2 receptors augment GluD1R-channel current remains to be determined.
source: Whether these receptors, and other GqPCRs, augment GluD1R-channel current remains to be determined.
evidence: This is stated as an open question for future research.

claim: Dysregulation of the 5-HT signaling in neuropsychiatric disorders is well-established.
source: Dysregulation of the 5-HT signaling neuropsychiatric disorders is well-established.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Pharmacotherapies to boost serotonin signaling are common and often efficacious in some neuropsychiatric conditions.
source: Pharmacotherapies to boost serotonin signaling are common and often efficacious in some of these conditions.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Genetic association studies have identified GRID1 as a susceptibility gene for psychiatric conditions, including schizophrenia, major depressive disorder, bipolar disorder, autism spectrum disorder, and alcohol dependence.
source: Genetic association studies have identified GRID1 as a susceptibility gene for psychiatric conditions, including schizophrenia, major depressive disorder, bipolar disorder, autism spectrum disorder, and alcohol dependence (Edwards et al., 2012; Fallin et al., 2005; Griswold et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Edwards et al., 2012; Fallin et al., 2005; Griswold et al., 2012.

claim: Global Grid1 knock-out mice display abnormal social behaviors, including heightened aggression and decreased social interaction.
source: Global Grid1 knock-out mice display abnormal social behaviors, including heightened aggression and decreased social interaction, as well as altered emotional behaviors (Yadav et al., 2012) that are analogous to features of neuropsychiatric conditions in humans.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yadav et al., 2012.

claim: Global Grid1 knock-out mice display altered emotional behaviors that are analogous to features of neuropsychiatric conditions in humans.
source: Global Grid1 knock-out mice display abnormal social behaviors, including heightened aggression and decreased social interaction, as well as altered emotional behaviors (Yadav et al., 2012) that are analogous to features of neuropsychiatric conditions in humans.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yadav et al., 2012.

claim: Both 5-HT and non-5-HT/GABAergic dorsal raphe neurons are activated by aversive, anxiety or fear-producing stimuli.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that both 5-HT and non-5-HT/GABAergic dorsal raphe neurons are activated by aversive, anxiety or fear-producing stimuli (Seo et al., 2019; Silveira et al., 1993), with regional subpopulation specificity (Grahn et al., 1999; Grahn et al., 2019; Lawther et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Seo et al., 2019; Silveira et al., 1993.

claim: Activation of dorsal raphe neurons by aversive stimuli shows regional subpopulation specificity.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that both 5-HT and non-5-HT/GABAergic dorsal raphe neurons are activated by aversive, anxiety or fear-producing stimuli (Seo et al., 2019; Silveira et al., 1993), with regional subpopulation specificity (Grahn et al., 1999; Grahn et al., 2019; Lawther et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Grahn et al., 1999; Grahn et al., 2019; Lawther et al., 2015.

claim: GluDR have been characterized as scaffold proteins or synaptic organizers, regulating LTD, endocytosis and trafficking of AMPAR, formation of excitatory and inhibitory synapses, and spine density, independent of ion conduction through the pore.
source: GluDR have been characterized as scaffold proteins or synaptic organizers, regulating LTD, endocytosis and trafficking of AMPAR, formation of excitatory and inhibitory synapses, and spine density, independent of ion conduction through the pore (Fossati et al., 2019; Hirai et al., 2003; Schmid and Hollmann, 2008; Tao et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fossati et al., 2019; Hirai et al., 2003; Schmid and Hollmann, 2008; Tao et al., 2018.

claim: NMDAR are known to signal through non-ionotropic or 'metabotropic' mechanisms where ion conduction is not required, to regulate LTD, AMPAR endocytosis, and spine morphology.
source: Similarly, NMDAR are known to signal through non-ionotropic or 'metabotropic' mechanisms where ion conduction is not required, to regulate LTD, AMPAR endocytosis, and spine morphology (Dore et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dore et al., 2016.

claim: The ability of GluDR-channels to carry ionic current does not conflict with its known role as a synaptic organizer.
source: The ability of GluDR-channels to carry ionic current does not conflict with its known role as a synaptic organizer, but rather expands the similarities between NMDAR and GluDR.
evidence: This is reasoning based on the comparison with NMDAR.

claim: The largest obstacle in advancing the understanding of the ionotropic nature of GluDR is the lack of known agonist and inability to gate the intact channel.
source: The largest obstacle in advancing the understanding of the ionotropic nature of GluDR is the lack of known agonist and inability to gate the intact channel.
evidence: This is stated as a challenge in the field.

claim: In domain-swapped chimeric channels, agonist binding to the ligand-binding domain of AMPAR or KainateR opens the GluDR-channel pore and generates a substantial current.
source: In domain-swapped chimeric channels, agonist binding to the ligand-binding domain (LBD) of AMPAR or KainateR opens the GluDR-channel pore and generates a substantial current, but the LBD of GluDR on the pore region of AMPAR or KainateR-channels fails to generate current (Orth et al., 2013; Schmid et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Orth et al., 2013; Schmid et al., 2009.

claim: The LBD of GluDR on the pore region of AMPAR or KainateR-channels fails to generate current.
source: In domain-swapped chimeric channels, agonist binding to the ligand-binding domain (LBD) of AMPAR or KainateR opens the GluDR-channel pore and generates a substantial current, but the LBD of GluDR on the pore region of AMPAR or KainateR-channels fails to generate current (Orth et al., 2013; Schmid et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Orth et al., 2013; Schmid et al., 2009.

claim: Activation of metabotropic glutamate receptors produces an inward current carried by GluD1R-channels in heterologous systems and brain slices.
source: Two prior studies have demonstrated that in heterologous systems and brain slices, activation of metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluR) produces an inward current carried by GluD1R- (Benamer et al., 2018) or GluD2R-channels (Ady et al., 2014), concluding that mGluR activation triggers gating of GluDR channels.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Benamer et al., 2018 and Ady et al., 2014.

claim: In dorsal raphe neurons, GluD1R-channels are functional and open under basal conditions, carrying subthreshold, tonic Na+ current.
source: The congruous explanation of our results is that, in dorsal raphe neurons, GluD1R-channels are functional and open under basal conditions, carrying subthreshold, tonic Na+ current.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing NASPM-sensitive tonic current.

claim: Activation of α1-ARs modulates gating of GluD1R-channels and excites dorsal raphe neurons by increasing tonic GluD1R-channel inward current.
source: Activation of α1-ARs, by exogenous agonist or synaptic release of noradrenaline modulates gating of GluD1R-channels and excites dorsal raphe neurons by increasing tonic GluD1R-channel inward current.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing α1-AR-mediated increase in current.

claim: The kinetics of iGluR synaptic currents are controlled by the lifetime of the receptor-agonist complex and the rate of desensitization and deactivation.
source: In general, the kinetics of iGluR synaptic currents are controlled by the lifetime of the receptor-agonist complex and the rate of desensitization and deactivation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The presence of ambient levels of glutamate and glycine along with slow desensitization activate NMDAR to produce a tonic inward current.
source: The presence of ambient levels of glutamate and glycine along with slow desensitization activate NMDAR to produce a tonic inward current (Sah et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sah et al., 1989.

claim: Whether GluD1R function as ligand-gated receptor-channels that open in response to a chemical signal is not yet determined.
source: Our results demonstrate that GluD1R are functional ion channels, but whether they function as ligand-gated receptor-channels that open in response to a chemical signal, is not yet determined.
evidence: This is stated as an open question.

claim: It may be that an endogenous agonist needed for gating GluD1R is present in brain slices.
source: Reminiscent of times before the discovery of glycine as a necessary co-agonist at NMDAR (Johnson and Ascher, 1987; Kleckner and Dingledine, 1988), it may be that an endogenous agonist needed for gating is present in brain slices.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the history of NMDAR research.

claim: It is possible GluD1R-channels are gated by an intracellular factor or require expression of accessory or interacting protein.
source: Alternatively, it is possible GluD1R-channels are gated by an intracellular factor or require expression of accessory or interacting protein (Tomita, 2010).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning with citation to Tomita, 2010.

claim: Tonic activation of α1-ARs cannot explain the tonic inward current as α1-AR antagonism did not change basal whole-cell current.
source: Tonic activation of α1-ARs cannot explain the tonic inward current as α1-AR antagonism did not change basal whole-cell current.
evidence: This is inferred from the prazosin experiment showing no effect on basal current.

claim: The mechanism by which α1-ARs increase GluD1R-channel current remains to be described and may be distinct from the tonic activation.
source: The mechanism by which α1-ARs increase GluD1R-channel current also remains to be described and may be distinct from the tonic activation.
evidence: This is stated as an open question for future research.

claim: GqPCRs bidirectionally change NMDAR and AMPAR ionic currents, producing LTP and LTD, in part through a variety of distinct postsynaptic mechanisms.
source: It is well-established that GqPCRs, especially mGluR and mAChR, bidirectionally change NMDAR and AMPAR ionic currents, producing the two major forms of synaptic plasticity, long-term potentiation (LTP) and long-term depression (LTD), in part through a variety of distinct postsynaptic mechanisms (Hunt and Castillo, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hunt and Castillo, 2012.

claim: The duration of the α1-AR-EPSC (~27 s) is exceptional for any known synaptic current and more closely resembles the duration of short-term synaptic plasticity.
source: To our knowledge, the duration of the α1-AR-EPSC (~27 s) is exceptional for any known synaptic current and more closely resembles the duration of short-term synaptic plasticity; for instance, endocannabinoid-mediated short-term depression (Lu and Mackie, 2016).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with citation to Lu and Mackie, 2016.

claim: GqPCRs activate phospholipase C which hydrolyzes PIP2 into IP3 and diacylglycerol.
source: Canonically, GqPCRs activate phospholipase C which hydrolyzes the integral membrane lipid phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) into inositol triphosphate (IP3) and diacylglycerol.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: PIP2 stabilizes Kv7 channels such that PIP2 hydrolysis following mAChR activation accounts for inhibition of M-current.
source: PIP2 stabilizes Kv7 channels such that PIP2 hydrolysis following mAChR activation accounts for inhibition of M-current (Suh and Hille, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Suh and Hille, 2002.

claim: PIP2 inhibits TRPV4 channels, such that GqPCR-dependent PIP2 depletion allows for TRPV4 channels to open.
source: In contrast, PIP2 inhibits TRPV4 channels, such that GqPCR-dependent PIP2 depletion allows for TRPV4 channels to open (Harraz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Harraz et al., 2018.

claim: GqPCRs stimulate the production of the endocannabinoid, 2-AG, that can act directly on ion channels in the membrane.
source: By the same signaling cascade, GqPCRs stimulate the production of the endocannabinoid, 2-AG, that can act directly on ion channels in the membrane (Gantz and Bean, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gantz and Bean, 2017.

claim: One possibility is that α1-ARs modulate GluD1R-channels through membrane lipid signaling, involving PIP2, diacylglycerol, or 2-AG.
source: Thus, one possibility is that α1-ARs modulate GluD1R-channels through membrane lipid signaling, involving PIP2, diacylglycerol, or 2-AG, as it can take tens-of-seconds to minutes for ion channels to recover from modulation by membrane lipids (Gantz and Bean, 2017; Suh and Hille, 2002).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning with citations to Gantz and Bean, 2017; Suh and Hille, 2002.

claim: There may be direct modulation of GluD1R-channels by G protein subunits or activation of protein kinase signaling cascades.
source: Alternatively, there may be direct modulation of GluD1R-channels by G protein subunits or activation of protein kinase signaling cascades.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about possible mechanisms.

claim: The inclusion of BAPTA in the internal recording solution makes it unlikely that α1-ARs modulate GluD1R-channels via IP3 and calcium release from intracellular stores.
source: The inclusion of the calcium-chelator BAPTA in the internal recording solution makes it unlikely that α1-ARs modulate GluD1R-channels via IP3 and calcium release from intracellular stores (Hoesch et al., 2004).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental conditions with citation to Hoesch et al., 2004.

claim: In heterologous systems and constitutively open mutant GluDR-channels, the current reverses polarity around 0 mV.
source: In heterologous systems and constitutively open mutant GluDR-channels, the current reverses polarity around 0 mV (Zuo et al., 1997), akin to AMPAR- and NMDAR-channels, while our results show Erev of ~ −30 mV.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zuo et al., 1997.

claim: Space-clamp error in brain slices may contribute to the difference in Erev between heterologous systems and the current study.
source: While slow voltage-ramps were employed to minimize space-clamp error, we cannot rule out that some of the difference may be attributed to space-clamp error in brain slices, especially since the magnitude of subtracted current is small relative to total membrane current at depolarized potentials.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the experimental approach.

claim: There are many reports of inward currents produced by activation of many different GqPCRs with reversal potentials between −40 and −23 mV under different recording conditions.
source: However, there are many reports of inward currents produced by activation of many different GqPCRs with reversal potentials between −40 and −23 mV (Awad et al., 2000; Brown et al., 2002; Yamada-Hanff and Bean, 2013) under different recording conditions; a commonality that is unlikely to be accounted for by space-clamp error alone.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Awad et al., 2000; Brown et al., 2002; Yamada-Hanff and Bean, 2013.

claim: Measurements of GluD1R-channel properties may be subject to voltage-dependence of the signaling pathway between α1-ARs and GluD1R-channels.
source: Another important consideration is that our measurements may be subject to voltage-dependence of the signaling pathway between α1-ARs and GluD1R-channels.
evidence: This is stated as a consideration for interpreting the data.

claim: Measurements of the current-voltage relationship should be considered an estimate of the α1-ARs-GluD1R-channel signaling complex.
source: Taken together, measurements here should be considered an estimate of GluD1R-channels, and more precisely as the current-voltage relationship of the α1-ARs-GluD1R-channel signaling complex.
evidence: This is stated as a caveat for interpreting the data.

claim: The α1-AR-mediated depolarization of dorsal raphe neurons that drives action potential firing in vivo is carried by the mixed cation channel, GluD1R.
source: In summary, the α1-AR-mediated depolarization of dorsal raphe neurons that drives action potential firing in vivo is carried by the mixed cation channel, GluD1R.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all the experimental data.

claim: In addition to their role as a scaffold protein, GluD1R are functional ion channels that critically regulate neuronal excitability.
source: Thus in addition to their role as a scaffold protein, GluD1R are functional ion channels that critically regulate neuronal excitability.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all the experimental data.

claim: Many of the biophysical properties of the GluD1R-channel are like other members of the ionotropic glutamate receptor family.
source: Many of the biophysical properties of the GluD1R-channel are like other members of the ionotropic glutamate receptor family.
evidence: This is inferred from the biophysical characterization in Figure 2.

claim: Ion channel function of GluD1R may be prevalent and relevant to neuronal excitability and circuit function in different parts of the nervous system.
source: Given the widespread distribution of these receptors throughout the brain (Hepp et al., 2015), ion channel function of GluD1R may be prevalent and relevant to neuronal excitability and circuit function in different parts of the throughout the nervous system.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the widespread distribution of GluD1R with citation to Hepp et al., 2015.

claim: This study lays the foundation to investigate the ion channel function of GluD1R in excitatory GqPCR-dependent synaptic transmission and regulation of neuronal excitability.
source: This study lays the foundation to investigate the ion channel function of GluD1R in excitatory GqPCR-dependent synaptic transmission and regulation of neuronal excitability, expanding upon the wealth of knowledge of pharmacology and regulatory elements established for NMDAR and AMPAR signaling.
evidence: This is stated as the significance of the study.
